title: How to Make a Quick Herb‑Packed Chimichurri for Steak
meta_description: Level up your grill game with our recipe for a quick herb packed chimichurri steak. Learn the secret to fast chopping and bold, zesty flavor.
html:
There is nothing quite like a sizzling ribeye or flank steak topped with a vibrant, acidic, and garlicky sauce. Chimichurri is the gold standard for steak toppings because it cuts through the richness of the meat with a sharp, herbal punch. If you've avoided making it because of the tedious chopping, you're in luck. Making a quick herb packed chimichurri steak dinner is actually incredibly simple if you have the right tools and a few fresh ingredients.

The Secret to a Fast Prep

The most intimidating part of any chimichurri recipe is the knife work. Traditional recipes call for finely minced parsley and oregano, which can take ten minutes of repetitive chopping. To speed this up, I use Herb Scissors. These five-blade herb shears allow you to mince cilantro, chives, and basil (or parsley) in one snip, effectively quintupling your speed.

By using Herb Scissors, you avoid the bruising that often happens in a food processor, which can turn your sauce into a muddy paste. Instead, you get clean, distinct cuts that keep the herbs bright and fresh. Plus, the included cleaning comb makes it easy to clear out the stuck bits of greenery between batches.

Ingredients for Your Quick Herb Packed Chimichurri

For the best results, stick to fresh herbs. Dried herbs simply won't provide the zing required to balance a fatty piece of beef. Here is what you will need for a standard batch:

  • 1 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley (stems removed)
  • 1/4 cup fresh oregano or cilantro
  • 3-4 cloves of garlic, minced finely
  • 1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
  • 1 teaspoon dried red pepper flakes
  • Salt and black pepper to taste

Step-by-Step: Assembling the Sauce

Start by gathering your herbs. I recommend bunching the parsley and oregano together in your hand. Using your Herb Scissors, snip the herbs directly into a mixing bowl. Because the blades are parallel, you get a consistent mince without having to move the herbs around the cutting board constantly.

Once your herbs are prepped, stir in the minced garlic. I prefer to grate my garlic into a paste for a more integrated flavor. Pour in the red wine vinegar and red pepper flakes, stirring well to let the acid begin breaking down the garlic's raw bite. Finally, slowly whisk in the olive oil until the sauce is emulsified but still has a chunky, rustic texture.

Let the sauce sit at room temperature for at least 20 minutes. This allows the flavors to meld, turning a simple mixture of oil and vinegar into a complex, savory condiment.

Grilling the Perfect Quick Herb Packed Chimichurri Steak

While your sauce rests, it's time for the meat. For this pairing, I recommend a flank steak or a New York strip. Pat the meat completely dry with paper towels—this is the secret to getting a deep, caramelized crust. Season generously with coarse salt and cracked black pepper.

Get your grill or cast-iron skillet screaming hot. For a flank steak, sear for about 4-5 minutes per side for medium-rare. The key is to let the meat rest for a full ten minutes after it leaves the heat. If you slice it too early, the juices will run out, and your chimichurri will slide right off the steak.

Slice the steak against the grain into thin strips, then spoon a generous amount of the chimichurri over the top. The heat from the meat will slightly warm the sauce, releasing the aroma of the fresh herbs.

Tips for Storage and Variations

If you have leftovers, store the chimichurri in a glass jar in the fridge for up to a week. The oil acts as a natural preservative, though the color may fade slightly over time. If the sauce thickens too much in the cold, just stir in a teaspoon of warm olive oil to loosen it up.

Want to switch things up? Try adding a squeeze of fresh lime juice for a brighter, more Latin-inspired flavor, or stir in a tablespoon of capers for an extra salty, briny pop. No matter the variation, using the right tools like the Herb Scissors ensures you spend less time prepping and more time eating.

FAQ

Can I use a food processor instead of chopping by hand?

You can, but be careful. Food processors often over-process the herbs, turning them into a puree. For a traditional, chunky chimichurri, manual chopping or using multi-blade shears is the way to go.

Which vinegar is best for chimichurri?

Red wine vinegar is the classic choice because it provides a sharp, punchy acidity. If you don't have any, apple cider vinegar is a decent substitute, though it is slightly sweeter.

Do I need to peel the garlic?

Yes, definitely peel the garlic. For the smoothest texture, you can mince the garlic with a knife or use a microplane to grate it directly into the bowl.
